doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Welk as perfectionist bandleader and businessman
summary: Welk's strict appearance rules, shaping jazz players' styles, lack of formal training, and reliance on musical director George Cates.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: What was it — being in the Welk organization, was it a pretty tight ship that they ran?

Mr. Welk was a perfectionist music-wise, and he was very conscious of a person’s appearance on television, as well as their musical ability. And he always wanted to keep a very clean cut looking group on television and at that time he didn’t allow any beards or strange looking — well what was considered later the hippie style. He was very conscious of all that. And also he loved jazz music, but he had a tendency, when he got a few jazz people around, to try to sway their style a little bit to fit his thing. Well I think

his favorite instrument to feature was the clarinet. But of course he liked my trombone playing too. Now the clarinet, there was a lot of people that followed Pete Fountain in there. We had Peanuts Hucko and they had Henry Cuesta. Well all these other people, Lawrence would try to change their style a little bit. And they would get kind of perturbed at him. But some way or other, whatever I played he couldn’t find anything to change. So he never bothered me. I just could play anything and it seemed to please him. But he was a musical perfectionist. He had a real good ear for music. And technically he did not know much about music. He didn’t know how to write.

He didn’t do any arranging, as a matter of fact his beginning in music was a correspondence course on accordion. And he started out as a chicken farmer back in North Dakota, and he was a failure at that. And so he decided to take a correspondence course in accordion. And he started out in the business that way as a single. And finally he worked his way into operating a full size orchestra. And he was a smart businessman. That was his other big asset, besides having a good ear. But he relied on George Kates, he was the musical director of the television show. He relied on him to make any changes musically, if something didn’t suit him. If Lawrence didn’t like the way something sounded, he would ask George to change it. He was a nice man to work for. I had no problem with him.
